## 27 Abstract

## 28 Background

29 Cardiometabolic-based chronic disease (CMBCD) at an individual level results from complex interactions

30 among a multi-tiered network of sociodemographic, behavioral, and metabolic factors. Though a

31 consensus set of risk factors drives CMBCD, population context influences risk factor effects and

32 interactions. To better understand this phenomenon, we investigated the multi-tiered networking of

33 cardiometabolic variables across diverse populations using a comparative modelling approach.

34 Methods and Findings

35 Utilizing nationally representative cross-sectional data from 48 countries participating in the World

36 Health Organization “STEPwise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance” survey,

37 we learned country-specific Bayesian networks including sociodemographic, behavioral, and

38 cardiometabolic variables (adiposity, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cardiovascular disease).

39 By computing the structural Hamming distance between pairs of networks, we compared differences in

40 network structures across regions and country income levels. We then used the learned networks to assess

41 individual risk factor influences and interactions on cardiometabolic outcomes. Country-specific Bayesian

42 networks varied in terms of the risk factors directly and indirectly associated with the cardiometabolic

43 outcomes. Network structures differed significantly across regions (p = 0.023) but not across income

44 levels (p = 0.91). These results were robust to an alternative learning algorithm, network comparison

45 metric, and data imputation approach. Older age (60+ vs. 30-44 years old) was associated with a greater

46 increase in probability of obesity in Europe and Central Asia (+80%) compared to other regions. Higher

47 education was associated with increased probability of obesity (+53%), diabetes (+18%), and

48 hypertension (+2%) in South Asia but decreased probability of obesity (-10%), diabetes (-32%),

49 hypertension (-16%), and hyperlipidemia (-25%) in Middle East and North Africa. The interaction

50 between age and sex in predicting obesity was significant in the highest proportion of countries in Europe

## 54 Conclusions

55 These results revealed specific regional patterns of multi-tiered cardiometabolic risk structures,

56 emphasizing the need for regionally tailored public health strategies rather than applying generalized

57 consensus evidence-based models. Future research should explore the structural drivers of regional

58 differences in inter-relationships of cardiometabolic risk factors, drivers, and disease.

## 59 Introduction

60 Cardiometabolic-based chronic disease (CMBCD) imposes a growing global health burden,

61 disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries.[1-3] As posited by several models,

62 CMBCD is based on complex interactions of multiple tiers of sociodemographic, behavioral, and

63 metabolic factors. Specifically, the CMBCD model incorporates the interaction of three primary drivers

64 (genetics, environment, and behavior) and four secondary drivers (adiposity-, dysglycemia-,

65 hypertension-, and lipid-based chronic disease) for certain cardiovascular diseases (CVDs;

66 atherosclerosis, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation).[3] Importantly, these individual factors and their

67 associated disparities are influenced by tertiary drivers such as social (socioeconomic status, education,

68 housing, etc.), structural (policy and politics shaping individual context), and cultural determinants of

69 health.[4, 5] Though a consensus set of risk factors is globally recognized in driving CMBCD, population

70 differences in these drivers may impact how they interact to influence clinical cardiometabolic outcomes.

71

72 Previous epidemiological studies have reported the population attributable fraction (PAF) of CVD,[6-8]

73 myocardial infarction,[9] and diabetes[10] associated with common cardiometabolic risk factors and

74 compared those values across regions or country income levels. For example, Lin et al showed that while

75 the mortality rate of diabetes attributable to high body mass index and overall dietary habits was higher

76 than that attributable to other risk factors among countries of all income levels, the impact of other risk

77 factors – including household air pollution and a diet high in processed meats – differed by country

78 income level.[10] Yusuf et al showed in the INTERHEART study that nine risk factors together explained

79 the majority of myocardial infarction risk in all regions and ages, though the PAF of myocardial

80 infarction associated with each risk factor differed by region.[9] The PURE study, a global prospective

81 cohort study that investigated the PAF of CVD associated with various risk factors, demonstrated that

82 metabolic risk factors were the predominant CVD risk factors globally.[8] However, hypertension was

83 associated with the highest PAF in low- and middle-income countries, while hyperlipidemia was

84 associated with the highest PAF in high-income countries.[8]

86 The aforementioned studies have underscored that risk does not operate uniformly across settings, yet

87 they predominantly focused on individual risk factors. Moreover, none have utilized a network-based

88 approach to analyze the complex interactions among the multiple tiers of risk factors and compare these

89 inter-relationships across multiple countries. Bayesian networks (BNs) can address this research gap.

90 Specifically, BNs are probabilistic graphical models that represent variables (referred to as nodes) and the

91 conditional dependencies between them (referred to as edges) as a directed acyclic graph.[11-13] The

92 structure of these networks can be learned from data while also integrating prior knowledge in the form of

93 imposed or disallowed edges. Analysis of BN structures can reveal inter-relationships among variables,

94 and queries of the learned networks can demonstrate the relative impacts of one or more variables. As

95 such, BNs have been used in multiple studies of CMBCD, albeit in the context of a single country.[14-22]

96

97 In this study, we employed BNs to analyze nationally representative cross-sectional data from 48

98 countries and investigate how multi-tiered networks of variables associated with CMBCD varied across

99 settings. Specifically, we 1) learned country-specific BNs using sociodemographic, behavioral, and

100 cardiometabolic variables, 2) compared the topology of BNs grouped by region and income levels, and 3)

101 utilized the learned BNs to assess the interaction and impact of individual risk factors on clinical

102 outcomes.

139 Data imputation

140 After excluding datasets and variables with missingness greater than aforementioned thresholds, the

141 remaining missing values were imputed using a random forest algorithm[24] To optimize the out-of-bag

142 error, a range of values was tested for the two parameters that correspond to the number of trees in each

143 forest and the number of variables randomly sampled at each split. For each country, the parameters

144 resulting in the lowest out-of-bag error were used to impute the variables. See Supplementary Tables 3

145 and 4 for the proportions of missing variables and the imputation error.

147 Bayesian network structure learning

148 The 14 variables were organized into the following hierarchical order from highest to lowest tier: non-

149 modifiable sociodemographic variables (age, sex, and urban/rural residence), modifiable

150 sociodemographic variables (education and household income), behavioral variables (tobacco use, alcohol

151 use, dietary fruit and vegetable intake, and physical activity), cardiometabolic drivers (adiposity, diabetes,

152 hypertension, and hyperlipidemia), and CVD (history of CVD). Edge blacklists were defined to

153 incorporate prior knowledge and improve the causal interpretation of the resulting networks. Notably,

154 edges from lower-tiered variables to higher-tiered variables as well as edges among non-modifiable

155 sociodemographic variables were disallowed. Additionally, edges among the cardiometabolic drivers

156 were disallowed based on previous evidence regarding causal relationships among drivers.[3, 25]

157

158 For each country, a BN was learned using the hill-climbing algorithm with a bootstrap resampling

159 approach modified to incorporate survey weights. Hill-climbing is a commonly used score-based graph

160 structure learning algorithm that explores the space of possible directed acyclic graphs through sequential

161 arc addition, deletion, and reversal steps in order to optimize fit according to a specified score.[26, 27]

170 Comparison of network topology

171 After learning a BN for each country, the network topologies were compared by calculating the structural

172 Hamming distance (SHD) between each pair of networks. The SHD is the number of edge additions,

173 deletions, and reversals needed to transform one network into another.[30] This metric has been

174 previously used to compare learned BNs and quantify the difference between them.[31, 32] To analyze

175 the factors associated with similarity in network topology, SHD values were compared based on whether

176 the networks were from countries in the same or different World Bank region (East Asia and Pacific

177 [EAP], Europe and Central Asia [ECA], Latin America and the Caribbean [LAC], Middle East and North

178 Africa [MENA], South Asia [SA], or Sub-Saharan Africa [SSA]),[33] income level (low, lower-middle,

179 upper-middle, or high),[33] and year of collection (pre-2017 or post-2017). For comparisons of SHD

180 across regions, income levels, and years, unpaired two-sampled Wilcoxon tests were used, as the SHD

181 was not normally distributed according to the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality.

184 Given the learned BN structures, parameter learning was conducted using the corresponding dataset,

185 incorporating the STEPS survey weights with implicit probabilistic expert system (I-PES) estimators

186 suggested by Ballin and Vicard.[34, 35] Specifically, the I-PES estimator approximates the probability of

187 each node in the BN integrating the BN dependence structure by conditioning on the parents of the node.

191 Risk factor impact analysis

192 The learned BNs were then used for inference by using conditional probability queries to analyze the

193 relative impact of sociodemographic and behavioral risk factors on the risk of CMBCD. Specifically, one

194 of the nine sociodemographic and behavioral risk factors was instantiated to different values, and the

195 relative change in the probability of the most advanced form of each cardiometabolic condition (obesity

196 for the Adiposity node, diabetes for the Diabetes node, stage 2 hypertension for the Hypertension node,

197 hyperlipidemia for the Hyperlipidemia node, and presence of CVD for the CVD node) was measured for

198 each country. These queries were conducted using likelihood weighting, an approximate inference

199 algorithm based on Monte Carlo sampling, by generating 107 random samples. The median value of the

200 relative change for each cardiometabolic condition was then calculated across all networks by region.

201

202 Risk factor interaction analysis

203 To evaluate the interactions of risk factors, the per-country fitted BNs were used to generate a simulated

204 dataset of the same size as the original dataset. For a given pair of risk factors and cardiometabolic

205 condition, a “reduced” multinomial regression model was fitted with the risk factors as individual

206 predictors and the cardiometabolic condition as the outcome. A “full” multinomial regression model was

207 fitted adding an interaction term for the pair of risk factors as a predictor. To assess the overall

208 significance of the interaction of those risk factors in predicting the outcome variable, we compared the

209 “full” and “reduced” models using the likelihood ratio test; a p-value less than 0.05 was considered

210 significant. This approach has been used in multiple similar analyses to assess interaction effects.[36, 37]

## 238 Results

239 Dataset characteristics

240 This study analyzed 48 STEPS country datasets spanning six regions and three income categories (Figure

241 1, Supplementary Table 1). The largest representation came from the EAP region (14 countries) and the

242 lower-middle income group (20 countries).  The median sample size of included datasets was 2,674

243 (range 365-7,295), with a total sample size of 146,086 across all countries.

244

245 Fourteen model variables were defined and harmonized across datasets (Supplementary Figure 1,

246 Supplementary Table 2). All 14 variables were available in 15 of 48 country datasets; the most frequently

247 missing variable was urban/rural residence, absent in 25 country datasets (Supplementary Table 3).

248 Across available variables, average data missingness per dataset was 0.9-13.6% (mean 4.1%). The mean

249 out-of-bag error of the random forest imputation was 0.301 across all datasets (Supplementary Table 4).

313 and disease across 48 countries using standardized nationally representative data. We found that 1) the

314 learned country-specific BNs were more similar for countries in the same region; 2) the degree and

315 direction of influence of certain risk factors on cardiometabolic outcomes differed by region; and 3) the

320 Country-specific BNs of cardiometabolic risk factors and disease have been learned based on national

321 datasets in the United States,[15, 43, 44] Spain,[16, 17, 19] and Korea[18] and utilized for various

322 applications. Our analysis built on these prior studies by learning country-specific networks and then

323 comparing the network structures. Network structures for each country varied significantly in terms of

324 main risk factors associated with CMBCD outcomes, as well as the pathways through which modifiable

325 and non-modifiable sociodemographic risk factors influenced clinical outcomes. Whether these learned

326 networks reflect underlying differences in the causal mechanisms by which CMBCD develops in each

327 country depends on certain assumptions. We approximated these assumptions by including all relevant

328 variables available for each country survey while disallowing illogical directed edges and specific

329 directed edges among cardiometabolic outcomes not supported by the medical literature. Even if the

330 country-specific BNs learned from the data do not represent causal mechanisms, the network edges do

331 reflect the strongest statistical associations between the variables of interest and, thus, patterns in the

332 country-specific epidemiology of CMBCD. Therefore, our finding that the BNs of countries in the same

333 region were more structurally similar than those of countries in different regions is remarkable and

334 suggests specific regional effects interconnecting sociodemographic, behavioral, and cardiometabolic

335 variables in country-specific networks.

336

337 Beyond differences in the overall network structure, we also demonstrated regional differences in the

338 impact of risk factors and distinct interactions between pairs of risk factors on cardiometabolic outcomes.

339 Education and/or household income were inversely associated with the probability of obesity in SA and

340 SSA though not in other regions. This inverse association has been previously reported in countries of

341 lower socioeconomic development, which characterizes many SA and SSA countries.[45-47]

352 factors). Regardless of the explanation, the regional differences in the interplay of variables underlying

353 CMBCD have implications in strategies to address the growing disease burden. Seminal studies have

354 demonstrated that a consensus set of risk factors account for a large portion of conditions such as

355 myocardial infarction and CVD, amounting to generic prevention principles worldwide.[8, 9] However,

356 our findings indicate that prevention efforts could be strengthened by accounting for region-specific risk

357 factor effects and interactions, allowing interventions to more effectively target high-risk groups and

358 locally relevant drivers of CMBCD. This process is a critical aspect of “transculturalization” – the

359 adaptation of clinical practice guidelines and other evidence-based frameworks from one setting to

360 another in a manner that respects cultural and environmental differences.[49, 50]

361

362 On the other hand, certain patterns were present in all or most regions. Compared to all other risk factors,

363 age had the most significant influence on probability of diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia in

364 most regions. Meanwhile, never smokers and never drinkers had a higher probability of obesity than

365 current smokers and drinkers, respectively, in all regions. This association between tobacco use and

366 adiposity has been supported in some studies[51, 52] and refuted in others.[53] While the mechanism of

367 this association is debated, neurobiological changes in weight regulation with smoking are often

375 Strengths and Limitations

376 Our study has several strengths. To our knowledge, this study is the first to employ a country-specific

377 network approach to analyze the multi-tiered drivers of CMBCD and compare results across a large set of

378 countries. BNs uniquely allow modeling of the interdependencies among multi-tiered variables and the

379 indirect effects of proximal risk factors on downstream health outcomes, an advantage that has been

380 previously illustrated in the context of CMBCD.[44] Subsequent comparison of network topology extends

381 conventional analyses to understand how the inter-relationships among variables differ across countries.

382 Furthermore, this study asserts a notable methodological improvement compared to prior studies that

383 utilized BNs to analyze CMBCD using large datasets collected via complex sampling designs. While such

384 BN analyses disregarded the accompanying survey weights, we integrate validated methods into both the

385 structure and parameter learning stages to incorporate STEPS survey weights and ensure more accurate

386 estimation. Finally, in contrast to prior multinational studies that use pooled dataset to study

387 cardiovascular risk factors, our approach to separately learn networks based on each country dataset

388 provides nationally representative country-specific analyses. These learned country-specific BNs can be

389 used by researchers and policymakers to conduct theoretical experiments and simulate the impacts of

390 interventions.

391

392 In terms of limitations, while the STEPS dataset provided standardized data across multiple countries and

393 many variables to broadly define cardiometabolic drivers, there was limited data on certain outcomes.

398 longitudinal, data may have underestimated the impact of long-term behavioral factors such as diet and

400 tradeoff to the considerable scope and crucial cross-country standardization of the dataset. Finally, the

401 STEPS data was not available for all countries, a limitation more pronounced in specific regions and

402 income levels. Acknowledging that this may affect the averaged results, we included all regions and

403 income levels with data to provide as global of an analysis as possible.

404

405 There were important limitations of the BN methodology. Structure-learning algorithms prioritize the

406 strongest relationships to produce the best-fitting model. Consequently, weaker associations may be

407 excluded from the learned structure and, thus, will not be reflected in conditional probability queries

408 using the learned network. This likely explains the null effect of some risk factors on cardiometabolic

409 outcomes present in our conditional probability queries. Finally, BNs were originally conceived as a

410 generative model designed to simulate scenarios. Thus, there is limited literature on validated approaches

411 to conduct hypothesis testing using the results of model queries. Our study utilizes conditional probability

412 queries to illustrate the general trends on the impact of risk factors but not to make precise estimates of

413 metrics such as PAF or odds ratios.

414

415 In this comparative network analysis of cardiometabolic risk factors, drivers, and disease across 48

416 countries, we found regional patterns of multi-tiered cardiometabolic risk structures and differential

417 effects and interactions of specific risk factors. This finding emphasizes the need

418 for regionally tailored public health strategies to effectively target high-risk groups.

# Florid cutaneous morbilliform eruption in the setting of primary Epstein-Barr virus infection

**Authors:** Shahin A. Saberi; Anusha M. Kumar; Dale Davis; Vinod E. Nambudiri

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | bDepartment of Dermatology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | cDepartment of Pathology, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts

## Introduction

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a member of the Herpesviridae family, is a highly prevalent virus with a range of clinical presentations from asymptomatic infection to infectious mononucleosis (IM). IM occurs in a subset of primary EBV infections as a clinical syndrome typically involving fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and mucosal inflammation (tonsillitis and pharyngitis) with associated sore throat. In patients with EBV IM, generalized cutaneous manifestations can include persistent morbilliform eruptions in patients exposed to antibiotics or more subtle, transient morbilliform eruptions in up to 15% of unexposed patients—though other morphologies (eg, papulovesicular, petechial) can arise infrequently.1, 2, 3 Generalized cutaneous manifestations are primarily associated with EBV IM, not milder forms of EBV infections in adults. Herein, we present a patient with a florid cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction in the setting of an otherwise low-grade primary EBV infection and no other identified triggers.

## Case Report

A 37-year-old male without significant past medical history was admitted with a diffuse cutaneous eruption. Erythematous, pink-red papules coalescing into thin plaques appeared first on the dorsal hands, progressively spreading to involve the majority of his body surface area within days. Follicular accentuation was noted, and the eruption began to vesiculate on the bilateral forearms and abdomen. Notably, the papulovesicular eruption spared the palms, soles, and mucous membranes; the palms only demonstrated mild diffuse erythema (Fig 1). The patient described the rash as pruritic but not painful or burning. Aside from intermittent low-grade fevers and subjective chills, the patient was asymptomatic. The patient denied sore throat, cough, recent prescription or over-the-counter medication exposures, or any sick contacts. A complete blood count was notable for a leukocytosis (white blood cell count of 14.4 K/μL) with neutrophilic predominance (86.1%). The patient's liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. His C-reactive protein level was markedly elevated at 145.7 mg/L, while his erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal at 18 mm/h.

A broad infectious workup was completed. Blood and urine cultures did not grow any pathogens.

Testing for influenza A and B, SARS-CoV 2, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, parvovirus B19, human immunodeficiency virus 1 and 2, Treponema, Babesia, Rickettsia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Lyme, tularemia, Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, Strep pyogenes, and Mycoplasma indicated no infection or prior immunity. Serology for EBV demonstrated positive viral capsid antigen IgM, negative viral capsid antigen IgG, and negative EBV nuclear antigen IgG, consistent with primary EBV infection.

While the infectious workup was pending, 2 4-mm punch biopsies were performed on the left forearm for hematoxylin and eosin staining and direct immunofluorescence. Biopsy samples demonstrated acute spongiotic dermatitis with subcorneal and intradermal vesicle formation, and mixed inflammatory infiltrate comprising rare eosinophils, neutrophils, and perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammation on hematoxylin and eosin staining, as well as 3-to-4+ C3 and trace-to-1+ granular IgA and IgM localized to the walls of superficial microvessels on direct immunofluorescence (Fig 2). The patient received 1 125-mg dose of methylprednisolone intravenously followed by 60 mg of oral prednisone daily for 3 days, tapered by 10 mg every 3 days thereafter. Adjunctive treatment included fexofenadine 180 mg daily and topical triamcinolone 0.1% ointment as needed to the affected areas. Significant improvement in lesions was noted within 5 days of treatment, with near-complete resolution noted at an 8-week follow-up visit.

## Discussion

We present a case of a diffuse, pseudo-vesiculated morbilliform eruption in the setting of primary EBV infection without antibiotic exposure or evidence of IM. Other than intermittent fevers, the patient presented with no localizing symptoms.

Rarely, cutaneous lesions are the presenting sign of otherwise asymptomatic primary EBV infection—prior cases include a 20-month-old girl with Giannotti-Crosti syndrome4 and a 43-year-old male with a pityriasis lichenoides-like eruption.5 An underrecognized but striking presenting sign of primary EBV is vulvar ulceration.6 Additional hypersensitivity responses have been reported in children, including erythema nodosum and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis.7 However, a florid cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction-like eruption as the presenting sign of otherwise low-grade EBV infection has not previously been reported in adults.

The lack of atypical lymphocytes and negative Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization on biopsy suggests that our patient's cutaneous eruption was an inflammatory hypersensitivity response to EBV rather than the result of direct EBV infection of skin cells. EBV can induce a robust cytotoxic T-cell immune response, which may have led to a T-cell–mediated cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction in this patient. The patient's use of marijuana in the days preceding the onset of the rash may also be implicated. In patients with EBV infection, antibiotic-induced rashes are thought to result from transient alterations of the immune system which enhance the immune response to drugs and lead to delayed hypersensitivity reactions.8,9 Given the papulovesicular morphology of lesions, adult Giannotti-Crosti syndrome was considered, but we favored characterizing this presentation as a florid hypersensitivity given the prominent truncal involvement, mixed infiltrate on histology, and demographics of the patient—Giannotti-Crosti syndrome is classically an acrally-distributed pediatric eruption that may rarely occur in the adult population.10

This case demonstrates that a primary EBV infection can trigger a florid morbilliform eruption even in the absence of antibiotic exposure and expands our understanding of cutaneous manifestations of acute EBV. We are also reminded that in the context of clinical and/or pathological evidence of a cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction, a broad infectious workup is warranted when an obvious medication or alternate culprit is not identified.
